# Effect Size

## Effect Size

Effect sizes provide ways to estimate the magnitude of an effect

::: subpoint
○ Standardized, so we can compare differences across scales
:::

::: fragment
Cohen's $d$: measure of difference (not a test)

::: subpoint
○ Transforms to the *z*-scale, can interpret in standard deviation units
:::

::: {.subpoint .fragment}
○ Mathematically, looks like *t*-statistic equations but has *standard deviation* ($s$) in the denominator instead of *standard error* ($SE$).
:::
:::




## Cohen's *d*

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="28%"}
#### One Sample

::: fragment
$$ d = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s_x} $$
:::


::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%}
```{r}
mu_cty <- 30

cty_bar <- mean(mpg$cty)
cty_sd <- sd(mpg$cty)

(cty_bar - mu_cty) / cty_sd
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
#### Independent Samples

::: fragment
$$ d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p} $$
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%}

::: panel-tabset
### Pull Data
```{r}
four_cyl <- mpg |>
  filter(cyl == 4) |>
  pull(hwy)
eight_cyl <- mpg |>
  filter(cyl == 8) |>
  pull(hwy)
```


### Calculate $d$
```{r}
x_bar_four <- mean(four_cyl)
sd_four <- sd(four_cyl)
n_four <- length(four_cyl)
x_bar_eight <- mean(eight_cyl)
sd_eight <- sd(eight_cyl)
n_eight <- length(eight_cyl)

pooled_sd <- sqrt( 
  ((n_four - 1) * sd_four^2 + 
     (n_eight - 1) * sd_eight^2) /
    ((n_four - 1) + (n_eight - 1)) 
)
(x_bar_four - x_bar_eight) / pooled_sd
```
:::

:::


:::

::: {.column width="28%"}
#### Paired Sample

::: fragment
$$ d = \frac{\bar{D}}{s_D} $$
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%}
```{r}
differences <- mpg$cty - mpg$hwy

d_bar <- mean(differences)
d_sd <- sd(differences)

d_bar / d_sd
```
:::

:::
::::


## Cohen's *d*

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
#### One Sample

$$ d = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s_x} $$


::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%}
```{r}
effectsize::cohens_d(mpg$cty, mu = 30)
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
#### Independent Samples

$$ d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p} $$

::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%}
```{r}
four_cyl <- mpg |>
  filter(cyl == 4) |>
  pull(hwy)
eight_cyl <- mpg |>
  filter(cyl == 8) |>
  pull(hwy)

effectsize::cohens_d(four_cyl, 
                     eight_cyl)
```
:::


:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
#### Paired Sample

$$ d = \frac{\bar{D}}{s_D} $$

::: {.fragment style="font-size:85%}
```{r}
effectsize::cohens_d(mpg$cty, mpg$hwy, 
                     paired = T)
```
:::

:::

::::



## Risk and Odds

::::: {style="font-size:80%"}
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="85%"}
Biologists have studied which kinds of food helps chicks grow best. They randomly assigned newly hatched chicks into different feed type groups and measured their body weight in grams after six weeks. This is a subset of the data that labels chicks under 250g small chicks and chicks above 250g large chicks.
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="15%"}
![](https://mannapro.com/cdn/shop/articles/how-to-raise-baby-chickens_2x_b6a71ebc-2d08-4bdc-82b0-18ccf861c9bd.jpg?v=1740003489)
:::
::::

```{r}
#| echo: false
d <- read_csv(here::here("lab", "data", "lab_06", "chick_data.csv"))

tbl <- d |>
  mutate(total = small + large) |>
  mutate(across(c(large, small, total), as.character)) |>
  bind_rows(c(feed = "Total", large = sum(d$large), small = sum(d$small), total = sum(d$small + d$large))) |>
  select(Feed = feed, Small = small, Large = large, Total = total) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_style(gt::cell_text(weight = "bold"),
                gt::cells_column_labels()) |>
  gt::tab_style(gt::cell_text(weight = "bold"),
                gt::cells_body(rows = Feed == "Total")) |>
  gt::tab_style(gt::cell_text(weight = "bold"),
                gt::cells_body(columns = Total))
tbl
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
What is the risk of a chick being small if they were in the linseed group? Soybean?

::: fragment
$\text{Risk(small | linseed)} = \frac{8}{12} = 0.6\bar{6}$

$\text{Risk(small | soybean)} = \frac{9}{14} = 0.64$
:::
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
What are the odds of a chick being small if they were in the linseed group? Sunflower?

::: fragment
$\text{Odds(small | linseed)} = \frac{8}{4} = 2$

$\text{Odds(small | sunflower)} = \frac{1}{11} = 0.\bar{09}$
:::
:::
::::

:::::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
What is the risk ratio of a chick being small if they were in the linseed group compared to the soybean?

::: fragment
$\text{Risk ratio} = \frac{\text{Risk(small | linseed)}}{\text{Risk(small | soybean)}} = \frac{\frac{8}{12}}{\frac{9}{14}} = 1.03$
:::
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="50%"}
What is the odds ratio of a chick being small if they were in the linseed group compared to the sunflower?

::: fragment
$\text{Odds ratio} = \frac{\text{Odds(small | linseed)}}{\text{Odds(small | sunflower)}} = \frac{\frac{8}{4}}{\frac{1}{11}} = 22$
:::
:::
::::

:::::


::: {.my-callout .fragment .absolute bottom=210 right=0 width="400px"}
The odds of a chick being small is 22x greater if they are fed linseed compared to if they are fed sunflowers!
:::

# Power Analysis


## Power Analysis

*Power*: the proportion of times we'd correctly reject the null hypothesis $H_0$ when something else is true, over many hypothetical repeated experiments

*Power analysis*: the chance of correctly rejecting $H_0$ if $H_0$ is not the reality.

::: {.subpoint .fragment}
○ Given that our null hypothesis is $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$,
:::

::: {.subpoint .fragment}
○ How often would we correctly reject the null if $\mu$ was not $\mu_0$?
:::

[$\beta$: probability of incorrectly retaining the null when $H_0$ is false]{.fragment}

[$1 - \beta$: power (probability of correctly rejecting the null when $H_0$ is false)]{.fragment}


## Power Analysis

What can we change in power analysis?

::: fragment
| $1 - \beta$ | $N$         | $\alpha$           | $\delta$         |
|-------------|-------------|--------------------|------------------|
| Power       | Sample size | significance level | true effect size |
:::

::: fragment
If know three, can solve for the fourth. 
:::

::: fragment
Can manipulate potential values to create power curves for different combinations
:::


## Power Analysis

We can use the `pwr` package in `R` to conduct power analyses! For a *t*-test, 

`pwr.t.test(n, d, sig.level, power)`

<div class="subpoint">○ `n` = sample size **in each group** </div>

<div class="subpoint">○ `d` = true effect size </div>

<div class="subpoint">○ `sig.level` = significance level, $\alpha$ </div>

<div class="subpoint">○ `power` = power, $1 - \beta$ </div>

Specify exactly three of the four, it will fill in the fourth

<div class="subpoint">○ `alternative` = type of test, default is `"two.sided"` </div>


## Power Analysis

`pwr.t.test(n, d, sig.level, power)`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
pwr::pwr.t.test(n = 10, 
                d = 0.3, 
                sig.level = 0.05)
```
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
pwr::pwr.t.test(n = 50, 
                sig.level = 0.05,
                power = 0.8)
```
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
pwr::pwr.t.test(d = 0.3, 
                sig.level = 0.05, 
                power = 0.8)
```
:::
::::


## Power Analysis

Object contains a list of each argument, including the one it calculated

```{r}
power_test <- pwr::pwr.t.test(n = 30, d = 0.3, sig.level = 0.05)

power_test |>
  glimpse()
```

Can pull the calculated statistic out with `$`

```{r}
power_test$power
```


## Aside: Low-Powered Studies

::: {style="font-size:80%"}
One of the components of the **replication crisis** is low-powered studies combined with publication bias (studies with $p < .05$ tend to get published more than $p \geq .05$). Why?

[When studies have small sample sizes (and thus low power), their standard errors are large, because $SE = \frac{s_x}{\sqrt{N}}$.]{.fragment}

[When standard errors are large, it takes a *very large* effect size to "beat" the null. So, low-powered studies that do beat the null are going to report a larger effect size.]{.fragment}

[But when they're the only studies that get published (selection on significance), it *looks* like some effect is large in the literature, when in fact the rest of the distribution of effect sizes are left in the *file drawer*.]{.fragment}

[Low-powered studies will often yield null results, but when they do have a significant effect (by chance), the effect will appear large.]{.fragment}
:::

::: footer
[(Ioannis 2005, "Why Most Published Research Findings Are False")](https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371/journal.pmed.0020124), [(Gelman 2006, "What 'Power = .06' Looks Like")](https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2014/11/17/power-06-looks-like-get-used/)

:::

## Power Analysis

::::: {style="font-size:80%"}

Can create power curves by iterating over candidate values for one of the inputs and calculating the remaining.

Example: You are running a study that you believe has a true effect size of $\delta = 0.25$. You want to test your hypothesis with a *t*-test at $\alpha = .05$. What will your power be at varying levels of sample size $N$ per group? 

:::: {.columns .fragment}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
sample_sizes <- c(10, 30, 100, 300)
power_values <- map_dbl(
  sample_sizes, 
  function(sample_size) {
    pwr::pwr.t.test(
      n = sample_size, 
      d = 0.25, 
      sig.level = 0.05)$power
  }
)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
tibble(n = sample_sizes,
       power = power_values) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = power)) +
  geom_line() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1))
```

### Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
tibble(n = sample_sizes,
       power = power_values) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = power)) +
  geom_line()
```
:::

:::
::::

:::::

## Power Curves

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.code-stack}
```{.r code-line-numbers="2-3,9"}
sample_sizes <- c(10, 30, 100, 300)
power_values <- map_dbl(
  sample_sizes, 
  function(sample_size) { 
    pwr::pwr.t.test(
      n = sample_size, 
      d = 0.25, 
      sig.level = 0.05)$power
  }
)
```

::: {.fragment fragment-index="0" .code-overlay}
```{.r code-line-numbers="4"}
sample_sizes <- c(10, 30, 100, 300)
power_values <- map_dbl(
  sample_sizes, 
  function(sample_size) {
    pwr::pwr.t.test(
      n = sample_size, 
      d = 0.25, 
      sig.level = 0.05)$power
  }
)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index="1" .code-overlay}
```{.r code-line-numbers="5-8"}
sample_sizes <- c(10, 30, 100, 300)
power_values <- map_dbl(
  sample_sizes, 
  function(sample_size) {
    pwr::pwr.t.test(
      n = sample_size, 
      d = 0.25, 
      sig.level = 0.05)$power
  }
)
```
:::

:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**`map_dbl()`**: iterate over every item in `sample_sizes`, do something to it, and return a `double` (number with decimal points).

::: {.fragment fragment-index="0"}
**`function(sample_size)`**: defines a function, tells `map_dbl()` what we want to *do* to each `sample_size`.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index="1"}
**`pwr::pwr.t.test(...)$power`**: the same function we were using before.
:::
:::
::::

## Power Curves: Bonus

Let's you easily add more conditions, like "what if the effect size was different?"

:::: {.columns .fragment}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
power_values_df <- tibble(
  sample_sizes = seq(10, 500, by = 20)
) |>
  expand_grid(d = c(0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.4)) |>
  mutate(
    power = map2_dbl(
      sample_sizes, d,
      function(sample_size, d) 
        pwr::pwr.t.test(
          n = sample_size, 
          d = d, 
          sig.level = 0.05)$power
    )
  )
power_values_df |> head(4)
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot

#| fig-width: 5

#| fig-align: center

## Different Sample Sizes

What if we wanted to have different sample sizes in our *t*-test?

`pwr.t2n.test(n1, n2, d, sig.level, power)`

<div class="subpoint">○ `n1` = sample size for group one </div>

<div class="subpoint">○ `n2` = sample size for group two </div>

<div class="subpoint">○ Everything else the same! </div>

<div class="subpoint">○ Have to specify at least one of the `n` values </div>

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
pwr::pwr.t2n.test(n1 = 10,
                  n2 = 20,
                  d = 0.3, 
                  sig.level = 0.05)
```
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
pwr::pwr.t2n.test(n1 = 50, 
                  n2 = 25,
                  sig.level = 0.05,
                  power = 0.8)
```
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
pwr::pwr.t2n.test(n1 = 100,
                  d = 0.3, 
                  sig.level = 0.05, 
                  power = 0.8)
```
:::
::::


## Paired-Samples *t*-Test

What if we wanted to look at power for a paired-samples *t*-test? Back to the original function...

`pwr.t.test(n, d, sig.level, power, type)`

<div class="subpoint">○ `type` = default is `"two.sample"`, but can switch to `"paired"` </div>

<div class="subpoint">○ Everything else the same! </div>

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
pwr::pwr.t.test(n = 10, 
                d = 0.3, 
                sig.level = 0.05,
                type = "paired")
```
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
pwr::pwr.t.test(n = 50, 
                sig.level = 0.05,
                power = 0.8,
                type = "paired")
```
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
```{r}
pwr::pwr.t.test(d = 0.3, 
                sig.level = 0.05, 
                power = 0.8,
                type = "paired")
```
:::
::::


## Paired- vs. Independent-Samples

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
power_values_df <- tibble(
  sample_sizes = seq(10, 500, by = 20)
) |>
  expand_grid(d = c(0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.4)) |>
  expand_grid(type = c("two.sample", "paired")) |>
  mutate(
    power = pmap_dbl(
      list(sample_sizes, d, type),
      function(sample_size, d, type) 
        pwr::pwr.t.test(
          n = sample_size, 
          d = d, 
          sig.level = 0.05,
          type = type)$power
    )
  )
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.panel-tabset}
### Plot
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
power_values_df |>
  mutate(d = factor(d)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sample_sizes, y = power, 
             color = d, group = d)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0.8), 
             linetype = "dashed", color = "gray75") +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap("type") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14)
```

### Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
power_values_df |>
  mutate(d = factor(d)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sample_sizes, y = power, 
             color = d, group = d)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0.8), 
             linetype = "dashed", color = "gray75") +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap("type") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14)
```
:::
